connection: Session 17 fixed a real encapsulation gap. This session studies the real interfaces already driving this codebase's polymorphism -- IClockEntryRepository, IClockEntryService, IEmployeeRepository, IEmployeeService -- plus IHoursPolicy's two swappable implementations, StandardHoursPolicy and FlexibleHoursPolicy.
objectives: List all four real interfaces in PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain and their real implementing classes, including the real EmployeeRepositor typo.
Explain what 'polymorphism' means concretely for ClockEntryService: it depends on IClockEntryRepository, and works correctly regardless of which implementation Program.cs registers.
Swap StandardHoursPolicy for FlexibleHoursPolicy in a call site and confirm the caller's code does not change, only its behavior.
Explain why EmployeeRepositor's real class-name typo does not affect polymorphism at all -- the interface name is what callers depend on, not the class name.

visuals.title: Four real interfaces, four real implementations
visuals.explanation: IClockEntryRepository -> ClockEntryRepository, IClockEntryService -> ClockEntryService, IEmployeeRepository -> EmployeeRepositor (typo, real), IEmployeeService -> EmployeeService.

visuals.title: Callers depend on the interface, never the class name
visuals.explanation: ClockEntryService's constructor parameter is IClockEntryRepository -- it would compile and run identically no matter what the concrete class implementing it is named, typo or not.

visuals.title: Two IHoursPolicy implementations, one call site
visuals.explanation: IHoursPolicy policy = flexible ? new FlexibleHoursPolicy() : new StandardHoursPolicy(8m); -- the line that calls policy.GetVariance(...) never changes.

visuals.title: Polymorphism is resolved at the call, not the declaration
visuals.explanation: The actual GetVariance implementation that runs depends on which concrete object policy refers to at runtime, not on the declared IHoursPolicy type.

preQuiz.prompt: Does EmployeeRepositor's real class-name typo (missing the 'y' in Repository) affect how IEmployeeRepository consumers behave?
options: No -- consumers depend on the IEmployeeRepository interface and its GetEmployeeById method, never on the concrete class's name; the typo is cosmetic to anyone using the interface
Yes -- it would cause a runtime error every time GetEmployeeById is called
Yes -- the interface itself must share the same name as its implementation
preQuiz.explanation: This is a real, verified fact about the source: EmployeeRepositor's typo has shipped in production-adjacent code without breaking anything, precisely because C# does not require implementation class names to relate to their interface names at all.

preQuiz.prompt: What single line changes when swapping StandardHoursPolicy for FlexibleHoursPolicy at a call site that only ever calls policy.GetVariance(...)?
options: Only the line that constructs the policy object (new StandardHoursPolicy(8m) becomes new FlexibleHoursPolicy()) -- every line that calls policy.GetVariance(...) afterward is unchanged
Every line in the calling method needs to change
preQuiz.explanation: This is the entire value of programming against IHoursPolicy: the construction site is the only place that names a concrete type; every subsequent use goes through the interface.

preQuiz.prompt: How many real, distinct interfaces in PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain have exactly one concrete implementing class each?
options: Four -- IClockEntryRepository, IClockEntryService, IEmployeeRepository, IEmployeeService each have exactly one real implementation, confirmed by reading the source directly
Zero -- none of these are actually interfaces
preQuiz.explanation: Even with only one implementation each today, all four are still real interfaces, giving Session 20's dependency injection and Session 30's test doubles a seam to substitute against.

concept.title: Four real interfaces, verified against source
paragraphs: IClockEntryRepository (implemented by ClockEntryRepository), IClockEntryService (implemented by ClockEntryService), IEmployeeRepository (implemented by EmployeeRepositor -- the real typo), and IEmployeeService (implemented by EmployeeService) are the complete list of interfaces in this codebase, confirmed directly against the source files.

Every one of ClockEntryService, PayrollService, and Program.cs depends on these interfaces, never on the concrete class names -- this is why EmployeeRepositor's typo never had to be fixed for the application to work correctly.

concept.title: Polymorphism at a real call site: IHoursPolicy
paragraphs: IHoursPolicy has two real implementations: StandardHoursPolicy(decimal scheduledHours), which computes recordedHours - scheduledHours, and FlexibleHoursPolicy, which always returns 0m.

A caller holding an IHoursPolicy variable calls .GetVariance(recordedHours) without knowing or caring which implementation it actually is -- the correct GetVariance runs based on the object's real runtime type, not the variable's declared type.
concept.code:
IHoursPolicy policy = flexible ? new FlexibleHoursPolicy() : new StandardHoursPolicy(8m);
decimal variance = policy.GetVariance(7.5m);   // -0.5m or 0m, depending on which object policy actually is

concept.title: What would actually break polymorphism here
paragraphs: If ClockEntryService's constructor took the concrete ClockEntryRepository class instead of IClockEntryRepository, Session 30's test doubles (a fake repository implementing the same interface) would have nowhere to substitute in -- polymorphism is what makes substitution possible at all.
The four real interfaces exist specifically so Program.cs's DI registrations (Session 20) can choose which concrete class to wire up, and so tests can wire up a different one entirely.

lab.objective: Trace all four real interface/implementation pairs, and swap IHoursPolicy implementations at a call site to observe polymorphism directly.
lab.startingCondition: IClockEntryRepository, IClockEntryService, IEmployeeRepository, IEmployeeService, IHoursPolicy, and their real implementations already exist.
steps: List all four repository/service interface pairs and confirm each implementing class's real name, including EmployeeRepositor's typo.
Write a small test that resolves an IEmployeeRepository as EmployeeRepositor and confirm GetEmployeeById works despite the class-name typo.
Call HoursPolicyTests.Caller_uses_policies_polymorphically with both flexible=true and flexible=false and confirm the SAME calling code produces two different GetVariance results.
Write down what would need to change in ClockEntryService if it depended on ClockEntryRepository (the concrete class) instead of IClockEntryRepository.
lab.expectedBehavior: All four interfaces resolve to their real implementations correctly; the IHoursPolicy test demonstrates two different behaviors from one call site depending only on which object is passed in.
lab.validation: dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release

expectedFiles.why: Confirm the real interface and EmployeeRepositor's real typo'd implementing class.
Confirm both real IHoursPolicy implementations and their differing GetVariance behavior.
Publish synchronized lesson, lab, and quiz material.

review: All four real interface/implementation pairs are verified against source, including the real EmployeeRepositor typo.
IHoursPolicy's two implementations are demonstrated producing different results from identical calling code.
The connection between 'depend on the interface' and 'the typo never mattered' is made explicit, not left implicit.

postQuiz.prompt: If a third IHoursPolicy implementation were added tomorrow (say, OvertimeHoursPolicy), how many existing call sites that call policy.GetVariance(...) would need to change?
options: Zero -- any code written against the IHoursPolicy interface accepts any implementation without modification; only the code that decides WHICH implementation to construct would need updating
All of them -- every call site would need a new branch
Exactly one -- the interface declaration itself
postQuiz.explanation: This is the practical payoff of polymorphism: adding a new implementation is additive, not a breaking change to existing interface-typed code.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does EmployeeRepositor's typo matter for a code reviewer, even though it doesn't matter for runtime behavior?
options: It is a real, minor maintainability smell -- future readers searching for 'EmployeeRepository' by exact name will not find it, even though the code works correctly
It causes GetEmployeeById to return null
It prevents the class from implementing IEmployeeRepository
postQuiz.explanation: The lesson distinguishes correctness (unaffected) from maintainability (mildly affected) -- both are real, separate concerns worth naming honestly.

postQuiz.prompt: What would ClockEntryService lose if its constructor took ClockEntryRepository directly instead of IClockEntryRepository?
options: The ability for Session 30's test doubles (a fake repository) to substitute in during testing, and the ability for a future EF Core-backed repository (Session 31) to substitute in during production
Nothing -- ClockEntryRepository already implements every member ClockEntryService needs
postQuiz.explanation: Depending on the concrete class still compiles and runs today, but permanently forecloses substitution -- exactly the cost Session 20 discusses for dependency direction.

reflections: Why does 'the interface name matters, the class name doesn't' feel counterintuitive at first, given how often class names are chosen carefully?
Where else in this codebase besides IHoursPolicy could a second, alternative implementation plausibly be added without touching any existing call site?
What would you look for in a code review to confirm a new class is genuinely programmed against an interface, not accidentally coupled to one concrete implementation?
whatBreaks: Changing ClockEntryService's constructor to depend on the concrete ClockEntryRepository class instead of IClockEntryRepository would still compile today, but it would permanently prevent Session 30's test doubles and Session 31's EF Core-backed repository from ever substituting in without changing ClockEntryService itself. Renaming EmployeeRepositor to fix its typo would require no changes anywhere else in the codebase precisely because nothing depends on that class name directly -- proof, by omission, that the typo was always harmless to behavior.
summary: PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain has four real interfaces, each with one real implementation, verified directly against source -- including EmployeeRepositor's real class-name typo, which never mattered because nothing depends on implementation class names. IHoursPolicy's two implementations, StandardHoursPolicy and FlexibleHoursPolicy, demonstrate polymorphism concretely: one call site, policy.GetVariance(...), produces different results depending only on which object policy actually refers to at runtime.
